newsitem.title: USA: No idled aluminum capacity restart soon -Reynolds.
newsitem.headline: No idled aluminum capacity restart soon -Reynolds.

text.p: Reynolds Metals Co plans no quick restart of its idled capacity despite market fundamentals continuing strong into 1998, the company's chairman and CEO Jeremiah Sheehan said.
Some 20 percent of the company's primary aluminum capacity was still idled.
"We have no intention to restart that capacity in the short term," Sheehan told reporters. "We will wait to see when the market really needs that aluminum."
In the second quarter Reynolds shipped 432,000 tonnes of aluminum.

Sheehan was speaking to reporters after updating analysts on the company's restructuring which could improve next year's pre-tax earnings by as much as $200 million, or $2 a share, after a string of assets sales, head office layoffs, and debt reduction.

Sheehan said if Reynolds started up its idled potlines, Alcoa would follow suit and restart its spare capacity. Close to a million tonnes of additional primary aluminum a year would then come on the market, Sheehan said.
Market fundamentals were strong, he said.
"Inventories are falling and we expect that to be true next year," Sheehan said.
He agreed with analysts who forecast aluminum at 90 cents a lb in 1998, compared with LME cash price of 69 cents Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Reynolds would still be interested in buying Venezuelan state-owned aluminum and alumina assets with other partners, but did not expect the already-delayed privatization to go ahead this year, Sheehan said.
"That size of facility does not come on the market very often," Sheehan noted.
Kaiser Aluminum pulled out of its move to buy the McCook mill in Illinois after lowering their original offer price. "We would expect others to see more value in it," Sheehan added.
The sale of McCook, along with the Alabama rolling mill to Alcoa, due to be concluded before year end, and other assets, some as yet to be named, will raise $900 million, Sheehan said.
The money will be used to cut debt and save $70 to $75 million a year on interest payments in the short term, Sheehan said.
Reynolds has a small stake in the Nigeria smelter project whose start up has been put back several times.
"I would expect metal to flow to some degree later this year," Sheehan told reporters. "We have made money on it. We have been paid for technology and management."
